## Post 1 — hook  📎 fig2_verification_flow.png

Every AI output should come with a receipt.

Ours do: a ~1 KB JSON file proving every step followed the domain's rules —
and anyone can check it WITHOUT the model. No weights. No GPU. No API. No
trusting the vendor.

Last week: how we force the rules. Today: how we prove it. 🧵

> **Alt text**: Flow diagram titled "Anyone can check the receipt — without
> the model." An AI system generates output with per-step rule checking on,
> emitting the output plus a JSON receipt. An independent verifier holding
> only the rulebook and the receipt re-checks every step. Three verdicts:
> honest output passes; a single edited field is caught ("Cart" changed to
> "Mars" — flagged because Customer-has-Mars is not a rule); a substituted
> rulebook is caught by fingerprint mismatch.

## Post 2 — the problem

Right now, verifying that an AI followed the rules is faith-based.

Rerun it? Nondeterministic. Read the logs? The vendor wrote them. Trust the
benchmark? It measured a different question.

The output itself carries no evidence. That's the gap receipts close.

## Post 3 — what's in the receipt  📎 fig1_certificate_anatomy.png

Inside the receipt, for EVERY step of the output:

• where the system was
• what move it made
• where it landed
• whether that exact move is in the rulebook
• whether the enforcer had to override the model

Plus a fingerprint of the exact rulebook in force. ~1 KB of JSON.

> **Alt text**: Annotated JSON certificate titled "The receipt: what ships
> with every AI output." Fields highlighted: tlts_fingerprint (which rulebook
> was in force — any edit changes the hash), per-step records with
> state_in/label/state_out and an in_delta flag (is this move a rule),
> forced and masked_kl fields (where and how hard the enforcer overrode the
> model), and a summary with the soundness verdict.

## Post 4 — verification is trivial. That's the point.

Checking the receipt = re-checking each step against the rulebook. A few
dozen lines of code, milliseconds, runs anywhere.

Your auditor doesn't need a GPU. They need two text files.

Compare: auditing a model's weights to establish ANY behavioral guarantee.

## Post 5 — what it catches

We attacked our own receipts (real runs, not hypotheticals):

• Edit one field of an honest receipt ("Cart"→"Mars"): caught at step 0 —
that move isn't in the rulebook.
• Swap in a different rulebook: caught twice — fingerprint mismatch AND
per-step failures.

Forgery requires producing a fully valid trace. Which is the point.

## Post 6 — the health gauge  📎 fig3_trust_signal.png

Bonus: the receipt shows how often the enforcer had to OVERRIDE the model —
0% when the model knows the domain, 71% when it has wrong habits.

Both outputs are equally valid. But 71% says the rules are doing the
model's job. That's your signal to retrain — or to check the rulebook.

> **Alt text**: Bar chart titled "The receipt doubles as a health gauge."
> Percent of generation steps where the enforcer overrode the model's first
> choice: 0% for a well-calibrated model, 71% for a mis-calibrated one.
> Annotation notes both outputs are valid, but 71% means the rules did most
> of the work — retrain or fix the rulebook.

## Post 7 — receipts are free

The receipt costs nothing extra to produce.

The enforcement that guarantees validity (thread 1) already computes every
fact the receipt records — the certificate is a byproduct of generation,
not a bolted-on audit pass.

Guaranteed behavior and proof of it come from the same mechanism.

## Post 8 — a proposal

A norm we'd like to see: work claiming "our model follows structure X"
should ship certificates with its outputs, so reviewers can re-verify
claims without weights or compute.

We put a sample certificate + verifier in the repo. Attack it. That's an
invitation.

## Post 9 — where this goes

The bigger picture:

Certificates turn "the AI concluded X" into "the AI concluded X via these
steps, each licensed by this rule, verifiable by anyone."

That's the audit trail for AI actions & conclusions — layered on at
decoding time, no from-scratch retraining.

## Post 10 — the honest caveat + links

Same caveat as always, because it's load-bearing: the receipt proves
rule-COMPLIANCE, not rule-QUALITY. A bad rulebook yields certified-bad
behavior. The receipt at least makes which rulebook was in force public and
checkable.

Sample certificate + verifier:
github.com/MikeHLee/structure_of_clear_thinking

## Posting notes

- Post after thread 01; Post 1 references it ("Last week…") — adjust the
  timeframe to the actual gap and link thread 01 in a reply to Post 1.
- Post 8 is deliberately an invitation to attack — engage with replies that
  try; a broken-then-fixed verifier is a better story than an unexamined one.
- If asked "can't the generator just lie on the receipt?": the verifier
  re-derives validity from the rulebook, so a lying receipt must still
  describe a fully valid trajectory — at which point the OUTPUT is valid,
  which is what the guarantee claims. The receipt binds output to rulebook;
  it doesn't claim to bind output to a particular model. Say this plainly if
  it comes up.
- Add the arXiv link to Post 10 once the paper is up.
